content: Coca tea, also known as mate de coca, is an herbal tea made from the leaves of the coca plant. It is prepared by either submerging coca leaves directly in hot water or by using a tea bag containing the leaves. This tea originates from the Andes mountain range, particularly in Peru. To produce one gram of cocaine, approximately 500 grams of coca leaves are required. Due to the presence of stimulant alkaloids, coca tea provides an energy boost similar to that of coffee. Commercially, coca tea is often sold in tea bags, each containing about one gram of coca leaf. Similar to how coffee can be decaffeinated, coca tea can undergo a process to remove cocaine, known as decocainization. However, even after this process, a small amount of cocaine remains in the tea, approximately 4 milligrams per tea bag. This residual amount is low enough to comply with legal standards in the United States under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. In the 1980s, coca tea was used as part of treatment programs to help wean individuals off cocaine addiction. The coca plant, scientifically named Erythroxylum coca, belongs to the family Erythroxylaceae and is native to northwestern South America. It is also referred to as la Hoja de Coca (the leaf of coca) or Coca del Peru (coca of Peru). While the tea is sometimes called mate, it is not consumed through a straw like yerba mate but is instead drunk as a traditional tea. Coca tea is a natural product that retains the physical and chemical properties of the coca leaf. It meets the Technical Peruvian Standard and can be sold nationally in Peru, although its use is discouraged in part by the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. The tea has a greenish-yellow color and a mildly bitter flavor, somewhat similar to green tea but with a slightly sweeter, more natural taste. In South American culture, coca tea is widely consumed, particularly in the Andes region, where indigenous tribes use it for both medicinal and religious purposes. Drinking coca tea or chewing coca leaves enhances oxygen absorption in the blood, which helps alleviate altitude sickness. It also has notable digestive and carminative properties. In the context of tourism, coca tea is commonly served to travelers on the Inca Trail to Machu Picchu, as it is believed to relieve symptoms of altitude sickness. In Bolivia, where the city of La Paz is situated at nearly 4,000 meters above sea level, official visitors are traditionally welcomed with a cup of mate de coca. Notable figures such as Princess Anne and the late Pope John Paul II were reportedly served coca tea during their visits to the region.
